H1.text: A burning candle seems to lose mass. A rusting iron gate gets heavier. And pure water, from a river or a lab, is always the same.

H2.text: Three puzzles. Five old laws explain all of them.

H3.text: Aarav finds rust on his bicycle chain, and wonders.

H4.text: Did the chain gain mass, or lose it? And where did the change come from?

H5.text: By the end, you will know the five laws reactions obey.

P1.text: Over two hundred years ago, chemists began to weigh every reaction.

P2.text: What they found became the five laws of chemical combination.

P3.text: Law one. Conservation of mass. Matter can neither be created nor destroyed. Antoine Lavoisier put it forward in seventeen eighty nine.

P4.text: Weigh a reaction in a closed flask. The total mass before equals the total mass after.

P5.text: So the rusty chain is heavier. Iron took in oxygen and water from the air. The candle seems lighter only because its gases escape.

U1.text: Law two. Definite proportions, from the French chemist Joseph Proust.

U2.text: A given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight.

U3.text: Proust tested natural and lab made copper carbonate. Both had the same percentages of copper, carbon and oxygen.

S1.text: Law three needs our molecule bench. Hydrogen and oxygen can make two different compounds.

S2.text: In water, one oxygen atom shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms.

S3.text: In hydrogen peroxide, two oxygen atoms bond to each other, and each one also holds a hydrogen.

S4.text: Now weigh them. Two grams of hydrogen combine with sixteen grams of oxygen to make eighteen grams of water.

S5.text: The same two grams of hydrogen combine with thirty two grams of oxygen to make thirty four grams of hydrogen peroxide.

S6.text: John Dalton saw this pattern in eighteen oh three. It is the law of multiple proportions.

B1.text: Fix the hydrogen at two grams. Oxygen is sixteen grams in one, and thirty two in the other.

B2.text: Pause and think. What is the ratio of these oxygen masses, in small whole numbers?

B3.text: One to two! The masses of one element that join a fixed mass of the other are in a small whole number ratio.

D1.text: Laws four and five are about gases. Let's build them step by step.

D2.text: Step one. In eighteen oh eight, Gay Lussac found that gases react in simple volume ratios, at the same temperature and pressure.

D3.text: Step two. One hundred millilitres of hydrogen and fifty millilitres of oxygen give one hundred millilitres of water vapour. Two to one to two.

D4.text: Step three. In eighteen eleven, Avogadro said that equal volumes of gases, at the same temperature and pressure, hold equal numbers of molecules.

D5.text: Step four. So two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule give two water molecules. The oxygen molecule must split in two. It has two atoms.

T1.text: Remember this. Atoms are never lost. They join in simple, whole number ratios.

W2.text: Carbon forms two oxides. In carbon monoxide, twelve grams of carbon join sixteen grams of oxygen. In carbon dioxide, they join thirty two grams. Which law is this?

W3.text: Carbon is fixed at twelve grams in both.

W4.text: The oxygen masses are sixteen grams and thirty two grams.

W5.text: Sixteen to thirty two is one to two. A small whole number ratio.

W6.text: So this is the law of multiple proportions.

C1.text: Let's line up all five laws.

C2.text: Conservation of mass, Lavoisier. Total mass never changes.

C3.text: Definite proportions, Proust. Pure water always has one gram of hydrogen for every eight grams of oxygen.

C4.text: Multiple proportions, Dalton. Small whole number ratios.

C5.text: Gaseous volumes, Gay Lussac. Simple volume ratios.

C6.text: And Avogadro. Equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules.

X2.text: Some students say a burning candle breaks the law of conservation of mass, because the candle gets lighter.

X3.text: But its gases escape into the air. Burn it in a closed flask, and the total mass stays the same.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As questions to name the law behind some data, and short mass ratio numericals.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Element X forms two oxides. In one, four grams of X join one point six grams of oxygen. In the other, two grams of X join one point two grams of oxygen. Find the ratio of oxygen masses for a fixed mass of X. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Two to three.

A2.text: First fix the mass of X. Double the second oxide, so four grams of X join two point four grams of oxygen.

A3.text: Now compare at four grams of X. One point six to two point four is two to three.

A4.text: A forgot to fix X first. That is the trap.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does a rusty iron chain weigh more than the clean chain?

Y3.text: Two. In pure water, what is the mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen?

Y4.text: Three. What did Avogadro say about equal volumes of gases?

N1.text: Next time: what is an atom, and why does it never break in a reaction? We find out in Dalton's atomic theory.
